en.q: The basic purpose of insurance is to:
o: Transfer the risk of financial loss from an individual to an insurer
Eliminate all risk of financial loss for the insured, so that no losses ever occur
Allow the insured to collect more than the actual loss so that the insured can profit
Guarantee the policyowner a fixed rate of return on every premium dollar paid
en.e: Insurance transfers risk. The insurer pools many similar risks so the losses of a few are paid by the premiums of many.

en.q: Which type of risk is insurable?
o: Speculative risk, where there is a chance of gain or loss
Pure risk, where there is only a chance of loss or no loss
Gambling risk
Market investment risk
en.e: Insurers cover pure risks (such as death or illness). Speculative risks, like gambling or investing, are not insurable.

en.q: The law of large numbers states that:
o: Larger policies always cost less per $1,000 of coverage, so insurers prefer to write them
The larger the group of similar risks, the more accurately losses can be predicted
Large insurers can never become insolvent, so their policyholders never need a guaranty fund
All claims will be paid in full
en.e: Predictable losses let insurers set adequate premiums. That is why they insure large pools of similar risks.

en.q: For life insurance, insurable interest must exist:
o: At the time of the claim only
At the time of application
Every year the policy is in force
Only for business policies
en.e: Insurable interest is required when the policy is applied for. It does not have to exist when the claim is paid.

en.q: The tendency of people with higher risk to seek or keep insurance more than others is called:
o: Moral hazard
Adverse selection
Morale hazard
Indemnity
en.e: Underwriting protects the insurer against adverse selection by classifying and pricing risks correctly.

en.q: The four essential elements of a legal insurance contract are:
o: Offer and acceptance, consideration, competent parties, and legal purpose
A signed application, the first premium, a licensed agent, and a conditional receipt
A policy form, an attached rider, a written endorsement, and a named beneficiary
An insurer, an insured, a policyowner, and a beneficiary who has an insurable interest
en.e: All four elements are required for the contract to be legally enforceable.

en.q: In an insurance contract, the applicant's consideration is:
o: The insurer's promise to pay the death benefit when a covered loss occurs
The completed application and the payment of the initial premium
The agent's commission
The signed policy delivery receipt and the statement of good health at delivery
en.e: Consideration is the value each party gives. The insurer's consideration is its promise to pay covered losses.

en.q: Insurance contracts are called aleatory because:
o: Only the insurer signs them, so only the insurer is legally bound by their terms
The exchange of values is unequal and depends on an uncertain event
They are drafted entirely by the insurer, so ambiguities are read in favor of the insured
They can be canceled by either party at any time with written notice to the other
en.e: A small premium may lead to a large payment, or no payment at all, depending on whether a loss occurs.

en.q: Because the insurer writes the policy and the applicant can only accept or reject it, ambiguities are interpreted in favor of the insured. This makes the policy a contract of:
o: Indemnity
Utmost good faith
Adhesion
Conditional receipt
en.e: In a contract of adhesion, the drafter (the insurer) bears the risk of unclear wording.

en.q: An insurance policy is a unilateral contract, which means:
o: Both parties make legally enforceable promises
Only the insurer makes a legally enforceable promise
The insured must pay premiums for life
The agent can change the terms
en.e: The insured is not legally required to keep paying premiums, but the insurer must pay covered claims while the policy is in force.

en.q: Statements in an application that the applicant believes to be true to the best of their knowledge are:
o: Warranties
Representations
Concealments
Riders
en.e: Representations need only be true to the best of the applicant's knowledge. Warranties are guaranteed to be true.

en.q: Intentionally withholding a material fact that would affect the insurer's decision is called:
o: Representation
Waiver
Concealment
Estoppel
en.e: Concealment of material facts can allow the insurer to void the contract, usually within the contestable period.

en.q: The authority that the public reasonably believes an agent has, based on the insurer's actions, is:
o: Express authority
Implied authority
Apparent authority
Limited authority
en.e: Express authority is written in the agent contract; implied authority is what is needed to carry it out; apparent authority comes from appearances.

en.q: Premiums collected by an agent on behalf of an insurer must be handled in a fiduciary capacity. Mixing them with personal funds is called:
o: Rebating
Twisting
Commingling
Sliding
en.e: Agents must keep premium funds separate and forward them promptly. Commingling is prohibited.

en.q: The Medical Information Bureau (MIB) is used by insurers to:
o: Pay medical claims directly to doctors and hospitals on the insurer's behalf
Share underwriting information to help detect misrepresentation
Approve doctors
Sell health insurance policies directly to applicants who were declined elsewhere
en.e: MIB information alone cannot be the sole reason to decline an applicant.

en.q: Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, if an applicant is declined based on a consumer report, the insurer must:
o: Notify the applicant and identify the reporting agency
Keep the reason secret to protect the privacy of the consumer reporting agency
Charge a higher premium without notice and keep the reason confidential
Cancel all of the applicant's other policies with that insurer
en.e: Consumers have the right to know when a consumer report is used and to dispute inaccurate information.

en.q: A mutual insurance company is owned by its:
o: Stockholders
Policyholders
Agents
State government
en.e: Mutual companies usually issue participating policies that may pay dividends to policyholders.

en.q: An insurer incorporated in another U.S. state but doing business in your state is a:
o: Domestic insurer
Foreign insurer
Alien insurer
Fraternal insurer
en.e: Domestic: formed in this state. Foreign: formed in another state. Alien: formed in another country.

en.q: A conditional receipt given with the initial premium generally provides coverage:
o: Only after the policy is delivered and the applicant signs a statement of continued good health
From the application or medical exam date (whichever is later), if insurable as applied for
Even if the applicant is uninsurable
Only for accidental death
en.e: If the applicant qualifies as applied for, coverage is effective as of the application or exam date.

en.q: When a new life insurance policy will replace an existing one, the agent generally must:
o: Hide the replacement from the existing insurer until the new policy's free look period ends
Follow the state's replacement rules, including required notices and comparisons
Cancel the existing policy first so the applicant is never covered by two policies at once
Charge an extra fee
en.e: Replacement rules protect consumers from losing benefits. Unnecessary replacement may be twisting or churning.

en.q: Term life insurance provides:
o: Temporary protection for a specified period, with no cash value
Lifetime protection with level premiums and guaranteed cash value growth
Investment accounts only
Income for life to the insured, starting once the specified term period ends
en.e: Term is pure protection. If the insured outlives the term, no benefit is paid.

en.q: In level term insurance, the:
o: Face amount decreases every year to match a loan balance
Face amount stays the same during the term
Premium increases every month as the insured grows older
Policy builds cash value that is paid out at the end of the term
en.e: Level term keeps the same death benefit; premiums are often level for the term as well.

en.q: Decreasing term insurance is commonly used to:
o: Fund retirement income for the insured after the mortgage is paid off
Cover a debt that decreases over time, such as a mortgage
Build cash value that can later be borrowed to pay down a mortgage
Pay for long-term care expenses that increase as the insured grows older
en.e: The face amount decreases over the term, matching a declining loan balance.

en.q: A renewable term policy allows the insured to:
o: Renew without evidence of insurability, at a premium based on attained age
Convert to an annuity
Renew coverage at the original issue-age premium after passing a new medical exam
Borrow against the cash value that builds up during each successive renewal period
en.e: Premiums increase at each renewal because the insured is older, but no new medical underwriting is required.

en.q: A convertible term policy allows the insured to:
o: Increase the face amount every year without any evidence of insurability
Change to permanent insurance without evidence of insurability
Receive annual policy dividends that reduce the premium for the rest of the term
Skip premiums
en.e: Conversion protects insurability: the insured can switch to whole life even after becoming uninsurable.

en.q: Whole life insurance provides:
o: Coverage for 20 years only, with premiums that increase at each five-year renewal
Lifetime protection with level premiums and guaranteed cash values
Flexible premiums and policyowner-directed investment choices in separate accounts
Coverage only for accidental death, with a double benefit for death on public transit
en.e: Whole life matures (endows) at a stated age such as 100 or 121 and builds guaranteed cash value.

en.q: In a limited-pay whole life policy, premiums are paid:
o: For a limited period (such as 20 years or to age 65), but coverage lasts for life
For the insured's whole life, but coverage ends once the insured reaches age 65
Only once
Only in the years the policyowner chooses, as long as the cash value covers the policy charges
en.e: Because premiums are compressed into fewer years, they are higher and cash value builds faster.

en.q: A single premium whole life policy:
o: Requires level premiums for life and builds cash value only after the third policy year
Is paid with one lump-sum premium and has immediate cash value
Has no cash value
Is a type of term insurance that is paid for with a single premium at issue
en.e: A single large premium creates immediate cash value; such policies are often modified endowment contracts.

en.q: Universal life insurance is known for:
o: Fixed premiums and a fixed death benefit, with cash value guaranteed to equal the face amount at age 65
Flexible premiums and an adjustable death benefit, with cash value earning current interest
Cash value invested only in mutual funds chosen by the policyowner, with no interest guarantee
Having no cash value
en.e: The policyowner can change premium payments and the face amount within limits; there is a guaranteed minimum interest rate.

en.q: Under universal life death benefit Option B (Option 2), the death benefit equals:
o: The face amount only, which stays level for the life of the policy
The face amount plus the cash value
The cash value only
The face amount plus all premiums paid to date
en.e: Option A is level (face amount); Option B is increasing (face amount plus cash value).

en.q: To sell variable life insurance, an agent needs:
o: Only a life insurance license, since variable life is regulated solely by the states
A life insurance license and a securities registration (FINRA)
A property and casualty license plus a state investment adviser license
No license
en.e: Variable products invest in separate accounts and are considered securities.

en.q: In variable life insurance, the cash value is invested in:
o: The insurer's general account, with a guaranteed minimum rate set at issue
Separate accounts chosen by the policyowner, so values can rise or fall
Government bonds only, with interest guaranteed by the insurer for the life of the policy
A savings account
en.e: The policyowner bears the investment risk. The death benefit typically has a guaranteed minimum.

en.q: A joint life (first-to-die) policy pays the death benefit:
o: When the first of the insureds dies
Only when both insureds die
When the youngest insured turns 65
Only for accidental deaths
en.e: Joint life covers two or more people and pays once, at the first death.

en.q: A survivorship (second-to-die) policy is often used for:
o: Mortgage protection, paying off the loan at the first death
Estate tax planning, paying at the second death
Paying for a child's college costs at the first death
Disability income for the surviving spouse after the first death
en.e: Survivorship life pays when the last insured dies, often when estate taxes are due.

en.q: Modified whole life insurance has:
o: Lower premiums for the first few years, then higher level premiums
Premiums that decrease every year until the policy is paid up at age 65
No premiums after the first year, because the policy is paid with a single premium
No cash value
en.e: Modified whole life helps people whose income is expected to grow, such as young professionals.

en.q: An accelerated (living) benefit rider allows:
o: Premiums to be paid faster so the policy becomes paid up early, like a limited-pay policy
The insured to receive part of the death benefit early if terminally or chronically ill
The beneficiary to receive double the face amount if the insured dies as the result of an accident
The policy to be converted to term insurance without evidence of insurability at any time
en.e: Any amount paid early reduces the death benefit paid to the beneficiary.

en.q: A guaranteed insurability rider allows the insured to:
o: Buy additional coverage at specified ages or life events without proof of insurability
Stop paying premiums after becoming totally disabled, following a six-month waiting period
Receive double the face amount if death results from an accident within 90 days of the injury
Cover a spouse
en.e: Typical option dates include certain birthdays, marriage or the birth of a child.

en.q: Credit life insurance:
o: Pays the insured's family
Pays off the insured's loan balance to the creditor, and cannot exceed the debt
Builds large cash values that the debtor may borrow against to repay the creditor
Is always permanent whole life insurance that builds cash value for the insured's family
en.e: Credit life is usually decreasing term, with the creditor as beneficiary.

en.q: Most group life insurance is issued as:
o: Whole life
Annually renewable term
Variable universal life
Endowment
en.e: Group life is usually yearly renewable term; members often may convert to individual coverage when leaving the group.

en.q: In indexed universal life, interest credited to the cash value is:
o: Fixed for the life of the policy at the interest rate the insurer declared at issue
Linked to the performance of a market index, usually with a minimum floor and a cap
Paid from separate accounts whose values rise and fall directly with the investments
Never credited
en.e: Indexed products offer some upside linked to an index while protecting against losses through a floor.

en.q: The entire contract provision states that:
o: The policy and a copy of the attached application make up the entire contract
The agent can add verbal promises later, as long as they are made before the policy is delivered
The insurer may change the policy terms at any time by mailing a written notice to the owner
Only the application matters if it conflicts with the policy, since the applicant signed it
en.e: Nothing outside the policy and attached application can be part of the contract, and the insurer cannot change it without the owner's consent.

en.q: After a life policy has been in force for a certain period (usually 2 years), the insurer cannot contest it for misstatements in the application. This is the:
o: Grace period
Incontestability clause
Free look provision
Reinstatement provision
en.e: After the contestable period, the insurer generally cannot void the policy because of misstatements, with limited exceptions.

en.q: During the grace period of a life insurance policy (commonly 30 or 31 days):
o: The policy is canceled and must be reinstated with evidence of insurability before coverage resumes
Coverage continues; if the insured dies, the unpaid premium is deducted from the benefit
Coverage is suspended, and no death benefit is paid unless the overdue premium was received
The premium doubles
en.e: The grace period prevents an unintended lapse for late payment.

en.q: If the insured's age was misstated on the application, the insurer will usually:
o: Void the policy and return the premiums, because age is a material fact in underwriting
Adjust the benefit to what the premium paid would have bought at the correct age
Pay double the face amount
Refund all premiums paid, with interest, and rescind the policy from its issue date
en.e: The misstatement of age provision adjusts benefits instead of canceling the policy.

en.q: Under a typical suicide clause, if the insured commits suicide within the first two years, the insurer:
o: Pays the full death benefit, since suicide is covered from the first policy day
Refunds the premiums paid instead of paying the death benefit
Pays half the death benefit and refunds the remaining premiums paid
Cancels coverage for the primary beneficiary and pays the contingent beneficiary instead
en.e: After the suicide exclusion period, suicide is covered like any other cause of death.

en.q: To reinstate a lapsed life policy (often within 3 years), the owner usually must:
o: Provide evidence of insurability and pay back premiums with interest
Apply for a new policy at the current attained age, with a new suicide exclusion period
Pay only the next premium due, with no evidence of insurability required
Wait 10 years
en.e: Reinstatement restores the original policy; a new contestable period may apply to the reinstatement application.

en.q: The free look provision allows a new policyowner to:
o: Skip the first premium
Return the policy within a set number of days for a full refund
Change the beneficiary without notifying the insurer during the first 30 days
Borrow the full face amount interest-free during the first 10 days
en.e: Free look periods are set by state law and are often 10 days, longer for some products and replacements.

en.q: If a policyowner dies with an outstanding policy loan, the insurer will:
o: Collect the unpaid loan from the beneficiary's own funds before paying the claim
Deduct the loan balance plus interest from the death benefit
Cancel the loan
Refuse to pay the claim until the beneficiary repays the loan balance
en.e: Policy loans are not required to be repaid, but any balance reduces the benefit.

en.q: The automatic premium loan provision:
o: Prevents a lapse by paying an overdue premium with a loan against the cash value
Increases the face amount automatically each year to keep pace with the cost of living
Pays premiums when the insured is totally disabled, after a six-month waiting period
Applies only to term insurance
en.e: It works only if the policy has enough cash value to cover the premium.

en.q: Which nonforfeiture option provides the same face amount as the original policy for a shorter period of time?
o: Cash surrender
Reduced paid-up
Extended term
Interest only
en.e: Extended term uses the cash value to buy term insurance for the full face amount. It is often the automatic option.

en.q: The reduced paid-up nonforfeiture option provides:
o: A lump sum of cash
A smaller amount of permanent coverage with no further premiums
The full face amount as term coverage for as long as the cash value lasts
An annuity for life, starting when the insured reaches the policy's maturity age
en.e: The cash value buys a paid-up whole life policy with a lower face amount.

en.q: Dividends paid on participating life insurance policies are generally:
o: Taxable as ordinary income
Considered a return of excess premium and not taxable
Guaranteed every year at the rate stated in the policy at issue
Paid only on term policies issued by stock insurance companies
en.e: Dividends are not guaranteed. Interest earned on accumulated dividends is taxable.

en.q: Under the interest only settlement option, the insurer:
o: Holds the death proceeds and pays the beneficiary only the interest earned
Pays the full amount immediately in one lump sum, including all interest earned
Pays the proceeds plus interest in equal installments over a fixed number of years
Pays income for the rest of the beneficiary's life, no matter how long the beneficiary lives
en.e: The principal can be paid later, for example to a contingent beneficiary.

en.q: A settlement option that pays the proceeds plus interest in installments over a specified number of years is:
o: Life income
Fixed period
Fixed amount
Lump sum
en.e: With fixed period, the time is set and the payment size is calculated. With fixed amount, the payment size is set.

en.q: The life income settlement option:
o: Pays installments for exactly 10 years, then stops even if the beneficiary is alive
Guarantees payments for as long as the beneficiary lives
Pays only the interest earned, while the insurer holds the principal
Is a lump sum
en.e: Life income works like an annuity for the beneficiary.

en.q: A contingent beneficiary receives the death benefit:
o: Before the primary beneficiary, if the contingent beneficiary is a minor child
Only if the primary beneficiary has died before the insured
Along with the primary beneficiary, in equal shares, in all cases
Only if the insured is still alive when the policy reaches its maturity date
en.e: The contingent (secondary) beneficiary is the backup to the primary beneficiary.

en.q: An irrevocable beneficiary:
o: Can be changed by the policyowner at any time, simply by filing a written change request with the insurer
Must consent before the owner can change the beneficiary or take actions such as policy loans
Has no rights at all
Is always the insured's estate
en.e: An irrevocable beneficiary has a vested interest in the policy.

en.q: Under the Uniform Simultaneous Death Act, if the insured and the primary beneficiary die at the same time and the order cannot be determined, the proceeds are paid:
o: As if the insured survived the primary beneficiary (to the contingent beneficiary or estate)
To the primary beneficiary's estate, as though the primary beneficiary had survived the insured
To the insurer
Equally to all relatives
en.e: This prevents the proceeds from passing through the primary beneficiary's estate.

en.q: A spendthrift clause protects:
o: The insurer from lawsuits filed by beneficiaries over delayed claim payments
Death proceeds from the beneficiary's creditors before they are paid
The agent from losing renewal commissions if the policy is later replaced
The policyowner from having to pay premiums after becoming totally disabled
en.e: It is used with installment settlement options to protect beneficiaries who may mismanage money.

en.q: The waiver of premium rider:
o: Doubles the death benefit if the insured dies in an accident within 90 days of the injury
Waives premiums if the insured becomes totally disabled, after a waiting period
Lets the insured buy additional coverage at set ages without proof of insurability
Pays the insured's medical bills
en.e: A typical waiting period is about six months, and premiums paid during it are often refunded.

en.q: The main purpose of an annuity is to:
o: Create an immediate estate at death for the beneficiaries named by the owner
Provide a stream of income, especially income that cannot be outlived
Pay medical expenses not covered by Medicare after the annuitant retires
Replace life insurance for young families who need a large death benefit at low cost
en.e: Life insurance creates an estate; an annuity systematically liquidates one.

en.q: During the accumulation period of a deferred annuity:
o: Premiums are paid and earnings grow tax-deferred
Income payments are made to the annuitant
The annuity cannot earn interest
Withdrawals are always tax-free
en.e: The annuitization (payout) period begins when the owner starts receiving income.

en.q: Under current federal law (SECURE 2.0), required minimum distributions from a traditional IRA generally must begin at age:
en.e: RMDs generally start at 73 for people who reach age 72 after 2022, rising to 75 later under the same law. Roth IRAs have no RMDs for the original owner.

en.q: An immediate annuity:
o: Is paid for with monthly premiums for 30 years before any income payments can begin
Is bought with a single premium, and income payments begin within one year
Never pays income
Is a type of term life insurance that pays a lump sum if the annuitant dies early
en.e: Immediate annuities are often called SPIAs (single premium immediate annuities).

en.q: Which annuity payout option pays the highest monthly income for a single annuitant?
o: Straight life (life only)
Life with 10-year period certain
Joint and survivor
Cash refund
en.e: Straight life pays only while the annuitant lives, with nothing left to beneficiaries, so it pays the most per month.

en.q: Under a life with period certain option, if the annuitant dies before the period ends:
o: Payments stop immediately, and the remaining balance is kept by the insurer
The beneficiary receives the remaining guaranteed payments
The insurer keeps all of the remaining funds as a mortality gain
The beneficiary receives double payments until the original period ends
en.e: Payments last for life, but are guaranteed for at least the period certain.

en.q: A joint and survivor annuity:
o: Stops all payments when the first of the two annuitants dies
Continues payments as long as either annuitant is alive
Pays only one lump sum
Covers more than ten annuitants, with payments split equally among them
en.e: Payments to the survivor may be the full amount or a reduced percentage, as chosen.

en.q: In a fixed annuity, the investment risk is carried by:
o: The insurance company
The annuitant
The agent
The beneficiary
en.e: Fixed annuities credit a guaranteed minimum rate, and the insurer guarantees the payments.

en.q: In a variable annuity, the investment risk is carried by:
o: The insurance company
The annuitant (contract owner)
The state guaranty fund
The agent
en.e: Variable annuities invest in separate accounts, and values rise or fall with the investments.

en.q: Surrender charges on an annuity:
o: Are charged only after age 65
Apply to withdrawals or surrender during the early years of the contract
Are a tax penalty
Never apply to deferred annuities, only to immediate annuities bought with a single premium
en.e: Surrender charges usually decline each year until they disappear.

en.q: Withdrawals of earnings from a nonqualified annuity before age 59½ generally face:
o: No tax at all
Ordinary income tax on the earnings plus a 10% penalty, unless an exception applies
Long-term capital gains tax on the earnings only, with no additional penalty
A 50% federal penalty on the entire withdrawal, including the owner's original principal
en.e: Exceptions include death and disability. The 10% penalty applies to the taxable portion.

en.q: Partial withdrawals from a nonqualified deferred annuity are generally taxed:
o: As earnings first (taxable), then as a return of principal
As a return of principal first (tax-free), then as taxable earnings
Never
At a flat 15% rate on the full amount withdrawn, regardless of earnings
en.e: This "last-in, first-out" treatment means gains come out first and are taxed as ordinary income.

en.q: The exclusion ratio determines:
o: The surrender charge that applies if the owner cancels during the early contract years
The portion of each annuity payment that is a tax-free return of principal
The amount of the death benefit paid to the beneficiary if the annuitant dies early
The agent's commission on each premium payment made during the accumulation period
en.e: The rest of each payment is interest (earnings) and is taxable.

en.q: Life insurance death benefits paid to a named beneficiary in a lump sum are generally:
o: Taxed as ordinary income
Not subject to federal income tax
Taxed as capital gains
Subject to a 10% penalty
en.e: Interest earned if proceeds are paid in installments is taxable, but the death benefit itself generally is not.

en.q: Premiums paid by an individual for personal life insurance are:
o: Fully tax-deductible
Not tax-deductible
Deductible only after age 65
Deductible as a business expense in all cases
en.e: Because premiums are not deductible, the death benefit is generally received income-tax free.

en.q: The growth of cash value inside a life insurance policy is:
o: Tax-deferred
Taxed every year
Taxed at a 50% rate
Taxed only if the insured dies
en.e: Gains are taxed only if the policy is surrendered for more than the owner's cost basis.

en.q: A life insurance policy that fails the "7-pay test" becomes a:
o: Term policy
Modified endowment contract (MEC)
Single premium deferred annuity (SPDA)
Group policy
en.e: Loans and withdrawals from a MEC are taxed as earnings first and may face a 10% penalty before 59½.

en.q: A Section 1035 exchange allows:
o: A tax-free exchange of an annuity contract for a new cash value life insurance policy
A tax-free exchange of a life insurance policy for another life policy or an annuity
Cashing out a policy without tax
Transferring a policy to a new beneficiary
en.e: Life to life, life to annuity, and annuity to annuity qualify. Annuity to life does not.

en.q: Qualified distributions from a Roth IRA are:
o: Fully taxable
Tax-free
Taxed at capital gains rates
Subject to a 10% penalty
en.e: Roth contributions are made with after-tax dollars, so qualified withdrawals are tax-free.

en.q: During the accumulation period, a variable annuity owner's account value is measured in:
o: Accumulation units
Annuity units
Shares of the insurer's stock
Dividend credits
en.e: During payout, the accumulation units are converted to annuity units.

en.q: Disability income insurance is designed to:
o: Pay hospital and surgical bills for injuries caused by an accident
Replace a portion of income lost because of a disability
Pay for nursing home and home health care costs after an illness
Provide a death benefit to the family if the insured dies from an accident
en.e: Benefits are usually limited to a percentage of earnings to keep an incentive to return to work.

en.q: In disability income insurance, the elimination period is:
o: The waiting period after the disability begins before benefits are paid
The period right after policy issue during which sickness is not covered
The maximum length of time that disability benefits will be paid for any one disability
The grace period for premiums
en.e: A longer elimination period lowers the premium. It works like a deductible measured in time.

en.q: Which definition of total disability is most favorable to the insured?
o: Any occupation
Own occupation
Any gainful employment
Presumptive disability only after 5 years
en.e: Under own occupation, the insured is disabled if they cannot perform the duties of their own job, even if they could do other work.

en.q: A residual disability benefit:
o: Pays only if the insured is totally disabled and unable to work in any occupation for at least a year
Pays a partial benefit for lost income when the insured returns to work with reduced earnings
Pays the full benefit forever
Is a type of life insurance
en.e: Residual benefits encourage returning to work by making up part of the income loss.

en.q: The probationary period in a health policy is:
o: The waiting period after a disability begins before income benefits start
A period after the policy is issued during which sickness is not covered
The time the agent has to deliver the policy and collect the first premium from the insured
The free look period during which the policyowner may return the policy for a refund
en.e: Probationary periods discourage people from buying coverage only after they know they are sick. Accidents are usually covered immediately.

en.q: An accidental death and dismemberment (AD&D) policy pays the:
o: Principal sum for accidental death and a capital sum for losses such as a limb or sight
Full principal sum for death from any cause, including illness, and half for losing a limb
Hospital bills only
Disability income for life
en.e: The capital sum is a percentage of the principal sum, depending on the loss.

en.q: Major medical insurance typically includes:
o: No deductibles or coinsurance, with first-dollar coverage on all medical bills
A deductible, coinsurance, and an out-of-pocket maximum
Coverage for dental care only
Fixed daily cash payments for each day spent in the hospital
en.e: Major medical covers a broad range of medical expenses with high benefit limits.

en.q: With an 80/20 coinsurance provision, after the deductible is met:
o: The insured pays 80% of covered expenses and the insurer pays the other 20%
The insurer pays 80% and the insured pays 20% of covered expenses
The insurer pays everything for the rest of the policy year with no cost sharing
The doctor writes off 20% of the bill and the insurer pays the remaining 80%
en.e: Coinsurance continues until the out-of-pocket maximum is reached.

en.q: Once the out-of-pocket maximum (stop-loss) is reached:
o: Coverage ends
The insurer pays 100% of covered expenses for the rest of the period
The insured pays 100% of covered expenses until the next policy year begins
Coinsurance switches to a 50/50 split for any covered expenses for the rest of the year
en.e: The out-of-pocket maximum limits the insured's total cost sharing for covered services.

en.q: In an HMO, members usually must:
o: Choose a primary care physician who acts as a gatekeeper and refers them to specialists
See any specialist directly without referrals and receive the same in-network benefit level
Pay full price for every visit
Use only out-of-network providers
en.e: HMOs emphasize preventive care and generally cover only in-network care except emergencies.

en.q: A PPO allows members to:
o: Use only in-network doctors, after getting a referral from a primary care gatekeeper
Use out-of-network providers, but at a higher cost than in-network ones
Avoid all deductibles and copays when using providers inside the preferred network
Skip premium payments
en.e: PPOs negotiate discounted fees with network providers; members pay less when they stay in-network.

en.q: A Health Savings Account (HSA) must be paired with:
o: Any HMO plan with a primary care gatekeeper and low copays
A qualified high-deductible health plan (HDHP)
A long-term care policy that is tax-qualified under federal law
A disability income policy with an elimination period of at least 90 days
en.e: HSA contributions are tax-advantaged and withdrawals for qualified medical expenses are tax-free.

en.q: Under the uniform mandatory provisions, the grace period for a health policy with monthly premiums is at least:
o: 7 days
10 days
31 days
60 days
en.e: The minimum is 7 days for weekly premiums, 10 days for monthly premiums, and 31 days for all others.

en.q: Under the time limit on certain defenses provision, after a health policy has been in force for a set period (typically 2 years), the insurer:
o: Cannot void the policy or deny a claim based on non-fraudulent misstatements in the application
Can cancel the policy for any reason, as long as it gives written notice and refunds the unearned premium
Must double the benefits
Can change the premium at will for any individual insured, as long as it gives 30 days' written notice
en.e: This is the health insurance counterpart of the life incontestability clause.

en.q: Under the notice of claim provision, the insured should notify the insurer of a claim within:
o: 24 hours
20 days of the loss, or as soon as reasonably possible
1 year of the loss, unless the insured lacked the legal capacity to notify
3 years
en.e: Notice of claim is followed by claim forms from the insurer and then proof of loss.

en.q: Under the uniform provisions, written proof of loss should generally be submitted within:
o: 10 days after notice of claim is given
30 days after the loss
90 days after the loss
5 years
en.e: If it is not reasonably possible, proof may be accepted later, generally up to one year, unless the claimant lacks legal capacity.

en.q: Under the legal actions provision, the insured cannot sue the insurer until:
o: 60 days after proof of loss is submitted, and not later than 3 years after proof is required
10 days after notice of claim is given, and not later than 1 year after the date of the loss
The policy is canceled
5 years after the loss
en.e: This gives the insurer time to process the claim before legal action.

en.q: Coordination of benefits is used to:
o: Increase the total benefits paid so that each plan pays its full benefit for the same covered claim
Prevent overinsurance under multiple group plans by naming one plan primary and the other secondary
Cancel duplicate policies
Set the deductible
en.e: The total paid by both plans cannot exceed the covered expenses.

en.q: Under the physical examination and autopsy provision, the insurer may:
o: Require the insured to pay for any exams the insurer orders, and require an autopsy in every death claim
Examine the insured at its own expense while a claim is pending, and request an autopsy where legal
Deny all claims without exams
Cancel the policy if the insured is found to be sick during any exam the insurer orders while a claim is pending
en.e: The insurer bears the cost of any examinations it requests.

en.q: Which provision allows the insurer to reduce benefits if the insured changes to a more hazardous occupation?
o: Grace period
Change of occupation
Reinstatement
Entire contract
en.e: If the insured moves to a less hazardous job, the insurer may reduce the premium instead.

en.q: In group insurance, the contract is issued to the employer as a master policy, and each covered member receives a:
o: Separate individual policy
Certificate of insurance
Conditional receipt
Buyer's guide
en.e: The employer (or other sponsor) is the policyholder. Members receive certificates describing coverage.

en.q: Group insurance underwriting generally:
o: Evaluates the group as a whole, usually without individual evidence of insurability
Requires a medical exam and a health questionnaire for every member before coverage starts
Is based only on the age and medical history of the oldest member in the covered group
Is not allowed by law
en.e: Underwriters look at the group's size, purpose, industry and makeup. Groups must not be formed just to buy insurance.

en.q: COBRA generally allows employees of employers with 20 or more employees to continue group health coverage after termination of employment for up to:
o: 6 months
18 months
5 years
Life
en.e: Some qualifying events for dependents allow up to 36 months. The individual may be charged up to 102% of the premium.

en.q: HIPAA is best known for:
o: Creating Medicare
Health coverage portability and protecting the privacy of health information
Regulating the commissions that life and health insurance agents may receive
Setting Social Security benefits
en.e: HIPAA restricts the use and disclosure of protected health information.

en.q: Medicare Part A primarily covers:
o: Inpatient hospital care
Doctors' services
Prescription drugs
Dental care
en.e: Part A also covers skilled nursing facility care after a qualifying hospital stay, hospice, and some home health care.

en.q: Medicare Part B primarily covers:
o: Inpatient hospital care
Doctors' services and outpatient care
Long-term custodial care in a nursing home
Prescription drugs only, through a private plan
en.e: Most people pay a monthly premium for Part B, plus an annual deductible and coinsurance.

en.q: Medicare Part C (Medicare Advantage) plans are:
o: Run only by the federal government, with no private insurers
Offered by private insurers approved by Medicare
The same as Medigap policies that supplement Original Medicare
Only for people under 65 who receive Social Security disability
en.e: Medicare Advantage plans provide Part A and B benefits, often with extra benefits and drug coverage.

en.q: Medicare Part D provides:
o: Hospital insurance
Long-term care
Prescription drug coverage
Disability income
en.e: Part D is offered through private plans approved by Medicare.

en.q: Which group of people is generally eligible for Medicare?
o: People 65 and older, some disabled people under 65, and people with end-stage renal disease
Only people with limited income and assets, regardless of age, through a joint federal-state program
Only veterans
Only people who have never worked and have no Social Security work credits of their own at all
en.e: Low-income assistance is mainly through Medicaid, a joint federal and state program.

en.q: Medicare supplement (Medigap) policies are designed to:
o: Replace Original Medicare entirely, with a private plan that covers all hospital and doctor bills
Help pay costs Original Medicare does not cover, such as deductibles and coinsurance
Cover only prescription drugs, replacing any need to enroll in a separate Medicare Part D plan
Be sold to people under 18
en.e: Medigap plans are standardized and identified by letters, so the same letter has the same core benefits from any insurer.

en.q: The Medigap open enrollment period is the:
o: First 30 days after age 70
Six months starting the month a person is 65 or older and enrolled in Medicare Part B
Any time the insured chooses
Annual enrollment period from October 15 to December 7 each year for all Medicare enrollees
en.e: During open enrollment, insurers cannot deny coverage or charge more because of health conditions.

en.q: Medicaid is:
o: A federal program only for people 65 and older, funded by payroll taxes and premiums
A joint federal and state program for people with limited income and resources
A private insurance plan sold by insurers to people who are not eligible for Medicare
Another name for Medigap coverage sold by private insurers to Medicare enrollees
en.e: Medicaid can pay for long-term care for people who meet its financial requirements.

en.q: Long-term care insurance benefits are commonly triggered when the insured:
o: Cannot perform a set number of activities of daily living (often 2 of 6) or is cognitively impaired
Has been in a hospital for at least three consecutive days immediately before entering a nursing home
Turns 65
Has a broken arm
en.e: Policies may cover nursing home care, assisted living, adult day care, and home health care.

en.q: Which of the following is an activity of daily living (ADL)?
o: Driving a car
Managing investments
Bathing
Shopping online
en.e: Common ADLs are bathing, dressing, eating, toileting, transferring, and continence.

en.q: Offering a prospect anything of value not stated in the policy as an inducement to buy is called:
o: Twisting
Rebating
Churning
Defamation
en.e: Rebating is illegal in most states, with limited exceptions allowed by some state laws.

en.q: Using misrepresentation to persuade a policyowner to drop a policy with one insurer and buy one from another is:
o: Twisting
Rebating
Commingling
Controlled business
en.e: Twisting is an unfair trade practice. Churning is a similar practice within the same insurer.

en.q: Repeatedly replacing a client's policies with the same insurer mainly to earn new commissions is called:
o: Rebating
Twisting
Churning
Sliding
en.e: Churning harms clients through new costs, new contestable periods and lost values.

en.q: Making false or malicious statements about an insurer's financial condition is called:
o: Rebating
Defamation
Misrepresentation of benefits
Coercion
en.e: Defamation of insurers is an unfair trade practice.

en.q: Which of the following is an unfair claims settlement practice?
o: Failing to promptly acknowledge and investigate claims
Paying a valid claim quickly, within the time frame required by state law
Requesting proof of loss from the claimant within the time limits set by the policy
Explaining in writing the specific reasons a claim was denied
en.e: State laws require insurers to handle claims promptly and in good faith.

en.q: The purpose of a life insurance Buyer's Guide is to:
o: Advertise a specific insurer's policies and compare its rates with competitors
Help consumers understand and compare types of life insurance
Replace the policy as the legal contract once it has been delivered to the buyer
Serve as a conditional receipt that gives temporary coverage until the policy is issued
en.e: State rules set when the Buyer's Guide and policy summary must be delivered to the applicant.

en.q: An insured becomes careless about personal safety because "the insurance will pay." This attitude is an example of a:
o: Moral hazard
Morale hazard
Physical hazard
Speculative risk
en.e: A morale hazard is indifference to loss because insurance exists. A moral hazard involves dishonesty or character flaws, such as filing false claims.

en.q: In insurance terms, the cause of a loss, such as an accident, an illness, or death, is called a:
o: Hazard
Risk
Exposure
Peril
en.e: A peril is what causes the loss. A hazard is a condition that increases the chance that a peril will occur.

en.q: Purchasing an insurance policy is an example of which risk management technique?
o: Transfer
Avoidance
Retention
Reduction
en.e: Insurance shifts the financial consequences of a loss to the insurer. Avoidance, reduction, and retention are the other basic methods of handling risk.

en.q: A large employer sets aside its own funds to pay employees' medical claims instead of buying a fully insured plan. This is an example of:
o: Risk avoidance by the employer
Reinsurance through another carrier
Risk retention (self-insurance)
Risk transfer to an insurer
en.e: Retaining risk means the organization pays its own losses. Self-insurance is a planned, funded form of retention.

en.q: When an insurer transfers part of a large risk it has accepted to another insurer, the arrangement is called:
o: Coinsurance
Reinsurance
Rebating
Assignment
en.e: Reinsurance lets an insurer accept larger risks while limiting its own exposure. The insurer that passes on the risk is the ceding company.

en.q: Policies that do not pay dividends to policyowners, typically issued by stock insurers, are called:
o: Participating policies
Fraternal policies
Assessment policies
Nonparticipating policies
en.e: Stock insurers are owned by stockholders, who may receive the company's profits as dividends. Owners of nonparticipating policies receive no policy dividends.

en.q: A nonprofit organization that provides insurance only to its members and operates through a lodge system with a representative form of government is a:
o: Fraternal benefit society
Reciprocal exchange
Stock insurer
Lloyd's association
en.e: Members of fraternal benefit societies typically share a common religious, ethnic, or social bond.

en.q: An insurer must obtain which document before it may transact insurance in a state?
o: A resident producer license
An approved buyer's guide
A filed policy summary form
A certificate of authority
en.e: An insurer holding a certificate of authority in a state is called an authorized, or admitted, insurer there.

en.q: The McCarran-Ferguson Act established that the business of insurance is regulated primarily by:
o: The federal government
The NAIC
The individual states
FINRA
en.e: Federal antitrust law applies to insurance only to the extent that the business is not regulated by state law.

en.q: The National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC) mainly:
o: Issues producer licenses that are valid in every state
Guarantees the claims of insurers that become insolvent
Sets the premium rates that all insurers must charge
Develops model laws and regulations that states may adopt
en.e: The NAIC promotes uniform regulation but has no direct regulatory power. Each state decides whether to adopt its models.

en.q: If an insurer becomes insolvent, its policyowners may be protected, up to limits set by law, by the:
o: State guaranty association
Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation
Medical Information Bureau
National Association of Insurance Commissioners
en.e: Guaranty associations are funded by assessments on insurers licensed in the state, not by the federal government.

en.q: The voluntary giving up of a known legal right is called:
o: Estoppel
Waiver
Rescission
Subrogation
en.e: Once a right has been waived, the legal doctrine of estoppel can prevent that party from later reasserting it.

en.q: An insurer issues a policy even though one application question was left unanswered. Regarding that question, the insurer is generally considered to have:
o: Kept the right to deny any claim related to it
Made the policy voidable at any time
Waived its right to the missing information
Required the beneficiary to answer it at claim time
en.e: By accepting the incomplete application, the insurer gave up its right to rely on the missing answer. Producers should make sure every question is answered.

en.q: An applicant gives an incorrect answer on a paper application and notices it before signing. The producer should:
o: Use correction fluid and write in the correct answer
Leave the error and explain it in a separate note
Correct it and have the applicant initial the change
Ask the underwriter to fix it after submission
en.e: Applicants must approve any change to their answers. Completing a new application is also acceptable; erasing is not.

en.q: The three primary factors used to calculate life insurance premiums are:
o: Age, income, and occupation
Mortality, interest, and expense
Face amount, commission, and taxes
Dividends, loans, and riders
en.e: Premiums reflect expected death rates, the interest the insurer expects to earn on its reserves, and its operating costs.

en.q: An applicant with a serious medical condition who is accepted for coverage at a higher-than-standard premium is classified as:
o: Preferred
Standard
Declined (uninsurable)
Substandard (rated)
en.e: Substandard risks may pay an extra premium or receive limited coverage. Preferred risks receive lower-than-standard rates.

en.q: An underwriter who wants details of an applicant's medical history directly from the applicant's doctor will request a(n):
o: Attending physician's statement
Inspection (character) report
Consumer credit report
Agent's field report
en.e: An attending physician's statement (APS) supplies medical records. Inspection reports focus on lifestyle, finances, and character.

en.q: Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, when an insurer orders an investigative consumer report on an applicant, it must:
o: Keep the report's existence hidden from the applicant until after underwriting
Obtain approval from the applicant's physician before ordering it
Disclose to the applicant in writing that the report may be made
Wait until the policy has been issued before telling the applicant about the report
en.e: Applicants also have the right to ask about the nature and scope of the investigation and to dispute inaccurate information.

en.q: No premium was collected with the application. When the policy is delivered, the producer should typically:
o: Leave the policy and return in 30 days for payment
Collect the initial premium and obtain a signed statement of good health
Ask the insurer to backdate coverage to the original application date to save age
Have the applicant sign a brand-new application
en.e: Coverage does not begin until the premium is paid. The statement of good health confirms the applicant's insurability has not changed since applying.

en.q: Life insurance is considered a valued contract rather than a contract of indemnity because it:
o: Reimburses only the actual economic loss proven by the beneficiary
Pays a stated amount regardless of the actual financial loss
Is valued by an independent appraiser after the insured's death
Pays only the cash value at death
en.e: Medical expense policies usually reimburse actual losses, while life policies pay the face amount stated in the contract.

en.q: A producer who represents the insurer is an agent. A producer who legally represents the insurance buyer is generally called a:
o: Solicitor
Underwriter
Broker
Adjuster
en.e: The distinction matters for legal responsibility. What an insurer's agent knows is generally considered known by the insurer.

en.q: A state insurance commissioner (director) generally has the authority to:
o: Examine insurers and suspend or revoke producer licenses
Pass new insurance laws on their own, without the state legislature
Set every insurer's dividend scale
Approve each individual claim payment
en.e: The legislature makes insurance law. The commissioner enforces it, issues licenses, and adopts regulations.

en.q: A return of premium term policy:
o: Builds guaranteed cash value just like whole life insurance does
Pays double the face amount if the insured dies during the term
Has the lowest premium of any type of level or decreasing term policy
Refunds the premiums paid if the insured outlives the term
en.e: The refund feature makes these policies more expensive than ordinary level term for the same face amount.

en.q: A family income policy provides a monthly income to the surviving family:
o: Starting at the insured's death and lasting for the rest of the surviving spouse's lifetime
From the insured's death until the end of a period measured from the issue date
Only if the insured dies after reaching normal retirement age
Only while the youngest child is enrolled full-time in college
en.e: It combines whole life with decreasing term. The later death occurs in the period, the fewer income payments remain.

en.q: A family policy (family plan) typically provides:
o: Permanent insurance on the primary insured and term coverage on the spouse and children
Term insurance on the primary insured and permanent whole life coverage on the spouse and children
Equal amounts of whole life coverage on every member of the family, including the spouse
Coverage on the children only, with no coverage on the parents
en.e: Children's coverage is often convertible to permanent insurance without evidence of insurability when they reach a certain age.

en.q: An accidental death benefit rider pays an additional amount when the insured dies in an accident, provided that death generally occurs:
o: Within 24 hours of the accident
Within a specified time after the accident, often 90 days
At any time, no matter how long after the accident it happened
Only while the insured is traveling for work
en.e: The time limit helps establish that the accident caused the death. A rider paying twice the face amount is often called double indemnity.

en.q: A payor benefit rider on a juvenile policy:
o: Pays the child's medical bills until age 18
Lets the child buy more coverage at age 21 or 25
Doubles the face amount if the child dies as the result of an accident
Waives premiums if the adult payer dies or becomes disabled
en.e: It keeps the child's coverage in force without further premiums. The adult payer usually must qualify for the rider.

en.q: A cost of living rider:
o: Increases the face amount in line with an inflation index
Reduces the premium gradually as the insured gets older
Pays a monthly income to the insured during retirement
Converts the base term policy into whole life coverage
en.e: It helps the death benefit keep its purchasing power. The increases are often provided through additional term coverage.

en.q: An endowment policy pays the face amount:
o: Only when the insured dies after reaching age 100
Only if the insured becomes totally and permanently disabled
When the insured dies or, if living, at the maturity date
In installments over the insured's lifetime only
en.e: Endowments build cash value quickly so that it equals the face amount at the maturity date, which makes premiums high.

en.q: A jumping juvenile policy is designed so that the face amount:
o: Decreases when the child reaches the age of 18
Is paid out automatically when the child turns 21
Increases at a set age, often to five times the original
Doubles only if the child becomes disabled before 21
en.e: The increase happens without evidence of insurability, and the premium does not change.

en.q: Industrial (home service) life insurance is characterized by:
o: Large face amounts with premiums paid only once a year by bank draft
Coverage sold only to employees of manufacturing firms
Benefits payable only when the insured's death results from an accident
Small face amounts with premiums collected frequently by an agent
en.e: It was designed for workers with modest incomes, often to cover final expenses.

en.q: Variable universal life insurance combines:
o: Fixed premiums with a guaranteed minimum interest rate
Level term insurance with a fixed deferred annuity
Flexible premiums with separate account investment choices
Whole life with a decreasing term rider attached
en.e: The policyowner bears the investment risk, so the producer needs both a life license and a securities registration.

en.q: A universal life policy uses death benefit Option A (level). As the cash value grows, the net amount at risk:
o: Increases
Decreases
Stays exactly the same
Equals the cash value
en.e: Under Option A the death benefit stays level, so a growing cash value makes up more of it and the insurer's pure insurance amount shrinks.

en.q: A universal life policy will lapse when:
o: The policyowner skips any single planned premium payment
The insured reaches age 65 with an outstanding loan
The credited rate falls to the guaranteed minimum
The cash value can no longer cover the monthly charges
en.e: Flexible premiums mean a missed payment does not automatically cause a lapse, but monthly deductions continue.

en.q: In a traditional whole life policy, the cash value equals the face amount:
o: When the policy matures (endows) at the maturity age
After the first ten policy years have passed
As soon as the first annual premium is paid
Only if dividends are used to buy paid-up additions
en.e: Whole life is designed so the cash value grows to equal the face amount at maturity, such as age 100 or 121.

en.q: For the same insured and face amount, which form of whole life has the lowest annual premium?
o: Limited payment whole life paid up in 20 years
Single premium whole life
Straight (continuous premium) whole life
Life paid-up at age 65
en.e: Spreading premiums over the insured's whole life keeps each payment lowest. Limited-pay policies compress premiums into fewer years.

en.q: In key person life insurance, the business is usually the:
o: Insured, owner, and beneficiary
Insured only
Owner, premium payer, and beneficiary
Beneficiary only, with the employee as owner
en.e: The key employee is the insured. The proceeds help the business recover from losing that person's skills or contacts.

en.q: In a cross-purchase buy-sell arrangement funded with life insurance, each business owner:
o: Buys and owns a policy on the life of each of the other owners
Buys a policy on his or her own life payable to the business
Relies on the business to own policies on all of the owners
Is covered under a group policy owned by the business
en.e: When an owner dies, the survivors use the proceeds to buy the deceased owner's share. In an entity plan, the business owns the policies instead.

en.q: In a split-dollar arrangement, an employer and an employee:
o: Each buy separate policies on each other's lives
Split the producer's commission on the policy evenly
Divide the employee's salary between two policies
Share the premiums and benefits under a written agreement
en.e: Split-dollar plans are a way to provide life insurance as an employee benefit, often to executives.

en.q: Under a Section 162 executive bonus plan, the employer pays the premium on a policy owned by the employee. The premium is generally:
o: Not deductible by the employer and not taxable to the employee
Deductible by the employer and taxable income to the employee
Taxable to the employer and deductible by the employee
Tax-free to both the employer and the employee
en.e: The premium is treated as additional compensation. The employee owns the policy and names the beneficiary.

en.q: The human life value approach determines the amount of life insurance based on:
o: The present value of future earnings the family would lose
The total of the family's current debts and nothing else
The insured's current net worth on the application date
A fixed multiple of the policy's annual premium
en.e: The needs approach instead adds up specific needs such as final expenses, debts, income replacement, and education.

en.q: An employee covered by group life insurance leaves the job. To convert to an individual policy without evidence of insurability, the employee generally must apply within:
o: 10 days
31 days
6 months
1 year
en.e: The new policy is permanent insurance at the attained-age rate. If the employee dies during the conversion period, the group benefit is paid.

en.q: A viatical settlement is:
o: A loan from the insurer against the policy's cash value for an ill insured
A settlement option chosen by the beneficiary after a death claim is approved
The insurer's refund of premiums after a suicide during the exclusion period
The sale of an ill insured's policy to a third party for less than face
en.e: The buyer becomes the owner and beneficiary and collects the death benefit when the insured dies. These transactions are regulated by the states.

en.q: For a young family with a limited budget and a large temporary need for protection, which type of policy provides the most death benefit per premium dollar?
o: Whole life
Universal life
Single premium whole life
Term life
en.e: Term insurance has no cash value, so the premium buys pure protection, making it the least expensive per dollar of coverage at first.

en.q: A policyowner surrenders a whole life policy for its cash value. Which statement is true?
o: Coverage continues for the original face amount
Coverage ends, and any amount received above the owner's cost basis is taxable
The beneficiary receives the cash value tax-free
The owner may reinstate it later without evidence of insurability within three years
en.e: Surrender ends the contract. The cost basis is generally the premiums paid minus amounts previously received tax-free, such as cash dividends.

en.q: Under the fixed amount settlement option:
o: Each payment amount is set, and payments last until funds run out
Payments are guaranteed for the beneficiary's whole lifetime
Only interest is paid, and the principal is kept intact
The number of years is fixed, and the payment size is calculated
en.e: Compare with the fixed period option, where the number of years is set and the insurer calculates the payment amount.

en.q: Which dividend option uses each dividend to purchase small amounts of permanent paid-up insurance?
o: Cash
Reduction of premium
Paid-up additions
Accumulation at interest
en.e: Paid-up additions increase both the death benefit and the cash value without evidence of insurability.

en.q: Under the one-year term dividend option, dividends are used to:
o: Reduce the premium due for the next policy year
Earn interest while left on deposit with the insurer until withdrawn
Buy additional paid-up whole life coverage
Purchase one-year term insurance, often up to the cash value
en.e: This is sometimes called the fifth dividend option. Any dividend left after the term purchase can be applied under another option.

en.q: Which person generally has the right to change the beneficiary, borrow against the cash value, and assign the policy?
o: The policyowner
The primary beneficiary
The insured, even if not the owner
The producer who sold the policy
en.e: Ownership rights belong to the policyowner, who may be someone other than the insured. An irrevocable beneficiary can limit some of these rights.

en.q: A policyowner uses a life policy as security for a bank loan through a collateral assignment. If the insured dies with the loan unpaid:
o: The bank is paid what is owed, and the rest goes to the beneficiary
The bank receives the entire death benefit regardless of the debt
The beneficiary must repay the loan from other funds first
The assignment makes the policy void and no benefit is paid
en.e: A collateral assignment is temporary and partial. An absolute assignment permanently transfers all ownership rights.

en.q: Under a typical assignment provision, the insurer is bound by an assignment only after it:
o: Has been approved by the beneficiary
Has been filed with the state insurance department
Has received written notice of the assignment
Has issued a replacement policy
en.e: The insurer is not responsible for the validity of an assignment, but it must know about it before it can honor it.

en.q: A policyowner names her three children as beneficiaries "per stirpes." One child dies before the insured, leaving two children of his own. That child's share will go to:
o: The insured's two surviving children
The deceased child's two children
The insured's estate
The contingent beneficiary named by the insurer
en.e: Per stirpes means "by the branch," so a deceased beneficiary's share passes to his or her descendants. Per capita divides the proceeds only among the living named beneficiaries.

en.q: The insured, who is also the policyowner, dies, and no named beneficiary is living. The death proceeds are generally paid to:
o: The state
The insurer's general account
The producer of record
The insured's estate
en.e: Proceeds paid to the estate may be delayed by probate and become subject to claims of the insured's creditors.

en.q: A policyowner names his eight-year-old son as beneficiary without setting up a trust. If the insured dies while the son is still a minor, the insurer will generally:
o: Pay the proceeds directly to the child in one lump sum
Pay the proceeds to the insured's closest adult relative
Pay the proceeds to a legally appointed guardian for the child
Deny the claim because a minor cannot be named beneficiary
en.e: Minors generally cannot legally receive and manage proceeds. Naming a trust or custodian in advance avoids delays.

en.q: A common disaster clause in a life policy:
o: Doubles the death benefit if the insured dies in a fire, flood, or other natural disaster
Requires the primary beneficiary to outlive the insured by a stated period
Excludes deaths caused by floods, earthquakes, and other natural disasters
Allows the beneficiary to be changed after the insured's death
en.e: If the primary beneficiary dies within that period, the proceeds go to the contingent beneficiary as if the primary had died first.

en.q: A policy's war exclusion uses a "results" clause. This means the insurer will not pay if:
o: The insured dies from any cause while in military service
The insured's death results from an act of war
The insured dies anywhere outside the United States
The insured served in the military before buying the policy
en.e: A status clause excludes any death while the insured is in military service, even from a non-war cause. A results clause is narrower.

en.q: The insuring clause of a life insurance policy:
o: Sets the premium amount and payment schedule
Explains when the policy becomes incontestable after issue
States the insurer's promise to pay the death benefit
Lists the riders attached to the policy
en.e: It is usually found on the first page and identifies the parties to the contract and the insurer's basic promise.

en.q: Which part of a policy states that the application and the payment of the premium are given in exchange for the insurer's promise?
o: Consideration clause
Insuring clause
Ownership provision
Free look provision
en.e: The consideration clause also typically states the amount and frequency of premium payments.

en.q: Which premium payment mode results in the lowest total yearly cost for the policyowner?
o: Monthly
Quarterly
Semiannual
Annual
en.e: More frequent modes cost more in total because the insurer has more administrative work and earns less interest on premiums received later.

en.q: A policyowner has an outstanding policy loan. If the loan balance plus accrued interest grows to exceed the cash value, the policy:
o: Automatically converts to extended term insurance for the net amount
Continues in force with no effect on coverage
Has the excess loan balance forgiven by the insurer
Will terminate after the insurer gives the required notice
en.e: Unpaid loan interest is added to the loan balance. A lapse with a large loan outstanding can also create taxable income.

en.q: A lapsed whole life policy generally cannot be reinstated if:
o: The policyowner can provide evidence of insurability
The lapse occurred within the past year
The policyowner surrendered the policy for its cash value
The overdue premiums are paid with interest
en.e: Once the cash value has been surrendered, the contract has ended. Reinstatement applies to policies that lapsed for nonpayment of premium.

en.q: Nonforfeiture options are required in permanent life insurance because:
o: The insurer must refund all premiums whenever the owner asks
Term policies build larger cash values than whole life policies
The cash value belongs to the owner and should not be lost on lapse
The beneficiary owns the cash value while the insured is alive
en.e: State nonforfeiture laws guarantee that the owner can take cash, reduced paid-up coverage, or extended term coverage.

en.q: A facility of payment clause, often found in industrial policies, allows the insurer to:
o: Delay payment of any death claim for up to one year after the date of death
Pay part of the proceeds to a person who is not the named beneficiary
Pay the producer's commission out of the death proceeds
Reduce the face amount by half if the insured dies within one year of issue
en.e: For example, the insurer may pay a relative or someone who paid the funeral expenses. It is useful when the beneficiary is a minor, has died, or cannot be found.

en.q: If the policyowner has not chosen a settlement option, the beneficiary usually:
o: Must accept the life income option chosen by the insurer
Receives only the interest earned on the proceeds
Must wait until the policy's maturity date to be paid
May take a lump sum or choose another settlement option
en.e: Lump-sum cash is the most common choice. An owner can instead select an option in advance and prevent the beneficiary from changing it.

en.q: An insured dies four years after a life policy was issued. The insurer discovers the applicant unintentionally failed to mention a past treatment for high blood pressure. The insurer will most likely:
o: Deny the claim and refund all of the premiums paid
Pay the death benefit since the contestable period has ended
Pay only half of the face amount to the beneficiary
Void the policy because of the application misstatement
en.e: After the contestable period, usually two years, the insurer generally cannot contest the policy for misstatements in the application.

en.q: A policyowner wants to be able to change the beneficiary at any time without anyone's consent. She should name a(n):
o: Irrevocable beneficiary
Revocable beneficiary
Tertiary beneficiary
Vested beneficiary
en.e: A revocable beneficiary has only an expectation of receiving the proceeds, not a vested interest, so the owner keeps full control.

en.q: In an annuity contract, the annuitant is the person:
o: Who sells the annuity contract to the owner
Who must always be the contract owner's spouse
Whose life expectancy determines the income payments
Who receives the death benefit if the owner dies
en.e: The owner, annuitant, and beneficiary can be different people. The owner holds the contract rights.

en.q: The owner and annuitant of a nonqualified deferred annuity dies during the accumulation period. Which statement is generally true?
o: The insurer keeps the account value as a mortality gain
The beneficiary receives all of the gain income-tax free
The beneficiary must wait until the annuitant's retirement age
The beneficiary is paid, and gains above cost basis are taxable
en.e: Unlike life insurance death benefits, annuity gains are not tax-free at death. They are taxed to the beneficiary as ordinary income.

en.q: Under a cash refund annuity, if the annuitant dies before receiving payments equal to the amount paid for the contract:
o: Payments continue to the beneficiary in installments until the balance is paid
The beneficiary receives the remaining balance in a lump sum
The insurer keeps the remaining balance
Payments continue for the beneficiary's lifetime
en.e: With an installment refund annuity, the balance is paid to the beneficiary as continuing payments instead.

en.q: When a variable annuity is annuitized, accumulation units are converted to annuity units. After that:
o: Both the number and the dollar value of the units are fixed for life
The number of annuity units is fixed, but their value varies
The number of units increases with every payment
Each payment is guaranteed never to change in amount after the first
en.e: Because unit values fluctuate with investment results, variable annuity income payments can rise or fall.

en.q: In a fixed indexed annuity, the participation rate is the:
o: Guaranteed minimum interest rate
Maximum rate of interest that can be credited to the contract in a period
Percentage of the index gain that is credited to the contract
Fee charged for an early surrender
en.e: For example, with an 80% participation rate and a 10% index gain, 8% would be credited, subject to any cap.

en.q: An annuity that lets the owner pay premiums of varying amounts at varying times during the accumulation period is a:
o: Single premium immediate annuity
Flexible premium deferred annuity
Life only annuity
Annuity certain
en.e: Single premium annuities are funded with one payment. Flexible premium annuities can be added to over time.

en.q: A fixed deferred annuity typically credits interest at:
o: A current rate that cannot fall below a guaranteed minimum
A rate tied directly to the gains of a stock index
The same rate as the owner's bank savings account
A rate that rises automatically with the owner's age
en.e: The insurer may declare a current rate above the minimum. The guaranteed rate protects the owner if interest rates fall.

en.q: An annuity certain (period certain only) pays income:
o: For the annuitant's lifetime only, with no guarantee
Until both of two joint annuitants have died
Starting only after the annuitant reaches age 85
For a specified period, whether or not the annuitant lives
en.e: Because it has no life contingency, an annuity certain does not protect against outliving one's income.

en.q: A variable annuity in the payout period uses an assumed interest rate (AIR) of 4%. If the separate account earns 7% during a period, the next income payment will generally:
o: Increase
Decrease
Stay the same
Stop
en.e: Payments rise when actual returns exceed the AIR and fall when returns are below it.

en.q: Income payments from a qualified annuity funded entirely with pre-tax contributions are:
o: Tax-free
Partially taxable using the exclusion ratio
Fully taxable as ordinary income
Taxed at long-term capital gains rates
en.e: Because the owner has no cost basis, there is no return of principal to exclude from tax.

en.q: For a Roth IRA withdrawal of earnings to be tax-free, the account generally must be at least five years old and the owner must:
o: Have reached age 59½ or meet an exception such as disability
Have reached age 55 and separated from service with the employer
Have made annual contributions for at least ten consecutive years
Have converted the account to a traditional IRA
en.e: Roth contributions themselves can be withdrawn tax-free at any time; the five-year and age rules apply to the earnings.

en.q: To keep a qualified retirement plan's tax advantages, the plan generally must:
o: Be offered only to the company's owners and officers
Invest its assets only in fixed annuity contracts
Allow withdrawals at any age without any tax penalty
Not favor highly compensated employees and meet IRS rules
en.e: Employer contributions to qualified plans are deductible, and employees are not taxed until they receive distributions.

en.q: A nonqualified deferred compensation plan:
o: Must cover all full-time employees on the same terms
Gives the employer an immediate tax deduction for the pay that is deferred
May cover only selected executives, with a delayed employer deduction
Must receive IRS approval before it can be offered
en.e: Because these plans do not meet qualified plan requirements, they may discriminate but lose the immediate deduction.

en.q: A 403(b) tax-sheltered annuity is available to employees of:
o: Any for-profit corporation of any size
Public schools and certain tax-exempt nonprofits
Sole proprietorships and partnerships only
Federal government agencies and the military
en.e: Eligible employers include public schools and 501(c)(3) organizations such as charities and churches.

en.q: A Keogh (HR-10) plan is a qualified retirement plan for:
o: Self-employed people and their eligible employees
Employees of public schools and colleges
Federal government civilian workers
Retirees over age 70 who no longer have any earned income
en.e: Self-employed people can make deductible contributions for themselves, but they must also cover eligible employees.

en.q: A Simplified Employee Pension (SEP) plan works by having:
o: Employees buy individual life insurance policies
The employer contribute to IRAs set up for each eligible employee
Employees make all contributions from after-tax pay into a company trust
The employer buy a group annuity for executives only
en.e: SEPs give small employers and the self-employed a simple way to make retirement contributions with little paperwork.

en.q: A person receives a distribution from a qualified plan and wants to roll it over to an IRA without paying tax. The rollover must generally be completed within:
o: 30 days
60 days
6 months
1 year
en.e: A direct trustee-to-trustee transfer avoids this deadline and the mandatory tax withholding that applies when the distribution is paid to the participant.

en.q: Loans from a life insurance policy that is not a modified endowment contract are generally:
o: Taxable as ordinary income when received
Subject to a 10% penalty before age 59½
Taxed as capital gains in the year received
Not taxable while the policy stays in force
en.e: If the policy lapses or is surrendered with a loan outstanding, part of the loan may become taxable.

en.q: A life insurance policy is sold to another person for value, and that buyer later collects the death benefit. Under the transfer-for-value rule, the proceeds are generally:
o: Entirely income-tax free regardless of the sale
Fully taxable with no deduction for the buyer's cost
Taxable to the extent they exceed the buyer's total cost
Subject to a 10% penalty on the whole amount
en.e: The buyer's cost is the price paid plus any premiums paid afterward. Certain transfers are exempt, such as a transfer to the insured or to a partner of the insured.

en.q: Life insurance death proceeds are generally included in the insured's gross estate for federal estate tax purposes when the insured:
o: Owned the policy or held incidents of ownership at death
Paid the premiums on a monthly basis
Was younger than age 65 at death
