Had named a beneficiary to receive proceeds under a settlement option
en.e: Incidents of ownership include the right to change the beneficiary, borrow, or surrender. Transfers of ownership within three years of death may also be included.

en.q: Employer-paid group term life insurance creates taxable income for the employee only for coverage that exceeds:
en.e: The cost of coverage above that amount, based on an IRS table, is added to the employee's taxable income.

en.q: Under annuity suitability and best-interest rules, before recommending an annuity a producer must:
o: Recommend the product that pays the highest commission to the producer
Get written approval from the state insurance commissioner for each sale
Make reasonable efforts to learn the consumer's finances and goals
Require the consumer to buy a life insurance policy first
en.e: The recommendation must reflect the consumer's profile, such as age, income, liquidity needs, risk tolerance, and tax status.

en.q: In a disability income policy, the benefit period is the:
o: Longest time benefits will be paid for one disability
Waiting period after the disability begins before any benefits start
Period during which premiums are being waived for the insured
Time allowed to submit written proof of loss after the disability begins
en.e: Benefit periods may last a few years or to a certain age, such as 65. Longer benefit periods cost more.

en.q: An insured recovers from a disability, returns to work, and becomes disabled again from the same cause within the time stated in the policy. Under a recurrent disability provision, the second period is:
o: A new claim that requires a new elimination period
Excluded from coverage as a pre-existing condition
Covered only if the insured buys a new policy
Part of the first claim, with no new elimination period
en.e: The time limit is commonly about six months. After that, a recurrence is treated as a new disability.

en.q: Under a presumptive disability provision, an insured is considered totally disabled after:
o: Missing more than 30 consecutive days of work
Changing to a less demanding, lower-paying job
The total loss of sight, hearing, speech, or use of two limbs
Being admitted to a hospital overnight for any illness or injury
en.e: Full benefits are paid even if the insured is able to work, because these losses are presumed to be totally disabling.

en.q: An individual buys a disability income policy and pays the premiums with after-tax personal funds. The disability benefits are:
o: Fully taxable as ordinary income
Generally received income-tax free
Taxable only after age 65
Taxed at capital gains rates
en.e: Because the premiums were not deductible, the benefits are not taxed. Benefits from employer-paid coverage are generally taxable.

en.q: Under a noncancellable health policy, as long as premiums are paid, the insurer:
o: Can raise the premium for one insured on an individual basis
Cannot cancel the policy or raise premiums above the policy rates
Can cancel the policy on any anniversary with written notice
Can reduce the benefits each time the policy renews
en.e: Noncancellable is the strongest renewability provision, which makes it the most expensive. It typically runs to a stated age, such as 65.

en.q: Under a guaranteed renewable health policy, the insurer must renew coverage but may:
o: Cancel the policy of a single insured whose health has gotten worse
Reduce the benefits at each renewal
Increase premiums, but only for an entire class of insureds
Increase premiums only for those individual insureds who file claims
en.e: Rate increases cannot target individuals. Guaranteed renewable policies generally cost less than noncancellable ones.

en.q: Business overhead expense insurance pays:
o: Business expenses such as rent and staff wages during disability
The disabled owner's own salary while unable to work
The cost of buying out a disabled partner's interest in the business
Lawsuits filed against the business by its customers
en.e: Premiums are generally deductible as a business expense, and the benefits are taxable income to the business.

en.q: A disability buy-sell (buyout) policy is designed to:
o: Replace the disabled owner's lost personal income
Pay the business's rent during an owner's disability
Pay the medical bills of a disabled business owner
Fund the purchase of a disabled owner's business interest
en.e: These policies usually have long elimination periods, often a year or more, and may pay a lump sum.

en.q: To qualify for Social Security disability benefits, a worker's disability generally must:
o: Prevent the worker from doing their own job for at least 30 consecutive days
Be caused by an accident that happened while on the job
Bar any substantial work and be expected to last 12 months or end in death
Begin after the worker reaches early retirement age of 62
en.e: The definition is strict, and there is a waiting period of five full months before benefits begin.

en.q: Workers' compensation pays benefits for:
o: Any illness, whether or not it is work related
Only injuries that happen while commuting to work
Disabilities caused by off-duty recreational sports
Injuries and illnesses that arise from employment
en.e: State laws require most employers to provide it. It pays medical expenses and lost wages for job-related injuries and illnesses.

en.q: A hospital indemnity policy pays:
o: A set daily amount while hospitalized, regardless of actual costs
The actual hospital bill in full, with no deductible or coinsurance
Benefits only for outpatient surgical procedures
The physician's surgical fees only, according to a fee schedule in the policy
en.e: Benefits can be used for any purpose, such as deductibles or household bills, because they do not depend on actual charges.

en.q: A critical illness (specified disease) policy pays benefits when the insured:
o: Visits any doctor for a routine annual physical exam
Is diagnosed with a condition named in the policy, such as cancer
Is injured in any type of accident, on or off the job
Reaches normal Social Security retirement age while the policy is in force
en.e: These policies supplement, rather than replace, comprehensive medical coverage.

en.q: Under the uniform reinstatement provision, a reinstated health policy covers accidents immediately and covers sickness that begins:
o: Immediately
After 30 days
After 10 days
After 90 days
en.e: This delay helps prevent people from reinstating coverage only after they become sick.

en.q: Under the uniform claim forms provision, if the insurer does not send claim forms within 15 days after receiving notice of claim, the claimant may:
o: Sue the insurer immediately for the full amount
Receive double benefits for that particular claim as a penalty
Submit written proof of loss in any form describing the loss
Cancel the policy and receive a full refund of all premiums paid
en.e: The proof must describe the occurrence, nature, and extent of the loss. This prevents the insurer from delaying a claim by withholding its forms.

en.q: Under the uniform time of payment of claims provision, periodic benefits such as disability income must be paid:
o: Only once a year
At least monthly
Only after the benefit period ends
At the insurer's discretion
en.e: Other benefits must be paid immediately upon receipt of due written proof of loss.

en.q: Under the illegal occupation optional provision, the insurer is not liable for a loss that results from the insured:
o: Changing jobs without notifying the insurer first
Holding more than one job at the same time
Working temporarily outside the United States
Committing a felony or working in an illegal occupation
en.e: A related optional provision lets insurers exclude losses resulting from intoxication or narcotics not taken on a physician's advice.

en.q: Under the Affordable Care Act, individual major medical plans:
o: May exclude pre-existing conditions for the first year
Cannot deny coverage or charge more because of pre-existing conditions
May charge higher premiums based on gender
May still set annual or lifetime dollar limits on essential health benefits
en.e: Premiums can vary only by limited factors such as age, location, tobacco use, and family size.

en.q: Under the Affordable Care Act, which metal tier pays the largest share of covered costs on average, generally with the highest premium?
o: Bronze
Silver
Gold
Platinum
en.e: On average, Platinum plans cover about 90% of costs, Gold about 80%, Silver about 70%, and Bronze about 60%.

en.q: A point-of-service (POS) plan combines features of HMOs and PPOs by:
o: Covering only care received from out-of-network providers
Using a gatekeeper while allowing costlier out-of-network care
Eliminating all deductibles, copays, and coinsurance
Paying providers only when members file their own claims
en.e: At the point of service, each time care is needed, the member decides whether to stay in the network.

en.q: HMOs often pay primary care physicians a fixed monthly amount for each enrolled member, regardless of the services used. This is called:
o: Fee-for-service
Coinsurance
Capitation
Indemnity
en.e: Capitation gives providers an incentive to keep members healthy and control costs.

en.q: Under the relation of earnings to insurance provision in a disability policy, if total benefits from all valid coverage exceed the insured's earnings, the insurer may:
o: Reduce its benefits proportionately and refund excess premium
Cancel the policy immediately without any notice to the insured
Double the elimination period for any future disability claims filed
Raise the premium retroactively to the original policy issue date
en.e: This optional provision helps prevent overinsurance, which could discourage the insured from returning to work.

en.q: A covered employee dies. Under COBRA, the employee's spouse and dependent children may generally continue the group health coverage for up to:
o: 6 months
18 months
29 months
36 months
en.e: Death of the employee, divorce, and a child losing dependent status allow up to 36 months. Termination of employment allows 18 months.

en.q: An employee is fired for gross misconduct. Under COBRA, the employee:
o: May continue coverage for 36 months
Is generally not eligible for continuation coverage
May continue coverage at no cost
Must be offered an individual policy by the employer
en.e: Termination for gross misconduct is the exception. Other voluntary or involuntary terminations are qualifying events.

en.q: In a noncontributory group plan, where the employer pays the entire premium, the plan generally must cover:
o: 100% of eligible employees
At least 50% of eligible employees
Only employees who request coverage
Only employees over age 40
en.e: Contributory plans, where employees share the cost, usually require a lower participation level, often 75%, to limit adverse selection.

en.q: An employee declines a contributory group life plan when first eligible and asks to enroll a year later. The employee will most likely have to:
o: Wait until age 65 to enroll
Provide evidence of insurability
Pay a penalty equal to a year of premiums
Buy an individual policy instead
en.e: Late enrollment raises adverse selection concerns, so the insurer may require proof of good health.

en.q: An employer pays the full premium for group disability income coverage. The benefits an employee receives are generally:
o: Tax-free
Taxable as income
Taxed at capital gains rates
Taxed only if paid for more than one year
en.e: Benefits are taxable to the extent the employer paid the premiums. If the employee pays with after-tax money, benefits are tax-free.

en.q: Employer contributions toward employees' group health insurance premiums are generally:
o: Deductible by the employer and not taxable income to employees
Not deductible by the employer and taxable as income to employees
Deductible by both the employer and the employees
Taxable to employees only after age 65
en.e: This favorable tax treatment is a major reason health coverage is commonly provided as an employee benefit.

en.q: Which type of care is generally not covered by Original Medicare?
o: Inpatient hospital stays
Doctors' services
Hospice care
Long-term custodial care
en.e: Medicare covers limited skilled nursing facility care after a qualifying hospital stay, but not ongoing help with daily activities. Long-term care insurance or Medicaid may cover it.

en.q: Medicare Part A generally covers care in a skilled nursing facility only if the patient:
o: Needs help only with custodial tasks such as bathing and dressing each day
Has lived in the facility for at least one full year before the claim
Needs skilled care after a hospital stay of at least three days
Is under age 65 and has no other health coverage
en.e: The qualifying stay must be as an inpatient. Coverage is limited in time, and the patient pays daily coinsurance after an initial period.

en.q: A Medicare Part A benefit period begins on the day a person is admitted as an inpatient and ends when the person has:
o: Been discharged from the hospital for at least one full day
Paid the annual Part B premium for that year
Reached the end of the calendar year of admission
Gone 60 days in a row without inpatient or skilled nursing care
en.e: A new benefit period, with a new Part A deductible, can begin after that. There is no limit on the number of benefit periods.

en.q: A person's initial enrollment period for Medicare Part B generally lasts:
o: Seven months, starting three months before the 65th birthday month
30 days, starting on the day of the 65th birthday
One full year, starting on the date the person retires from full-time work
Six months, starting on the day the person turns 64
en.e: Someone who delays Part B without other creditable coverage, such as current employer group coverage, may pay a late enrollment penalty for as long as they have Part B.

en.q: Medicare is administered at the federal level by the:
o: Social Security Administration alone
State insurance departments
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS)
National Association of Insurance Commissioners
en.e: Social Security handles much of the enrollment, but CMS runs the program and approves Medicare Advantage and Part D plans.

en.q: Every insurer that sells Medicare supplement policies must offer:
o: Plan A, which contains the basic benefits
Every lettered plan
A plan with prescription drug coverage
A plan with no premium
en.e: Plan A's basic benefits include coverage for Part A hospital coinsurance and Part B coinsurance. Insurers choose which other lettered plans to sell.

en.q: A client is enrolled in a Medicare Advantage plan and plans to keep it. A producer who knows this sells the client a Medigap policy. This sale is:
o: Required by federal law for every Medicare Advantage enrollee who is 65 or older
A way to lower the client's Advantage plan premium
A legal replacement for the client's Part D coverage
Generally illegal, since Medigap does not work with Advantage plans
en.e: Medigap works only with Original Medicare. A Medigap policy may be sold if the person is leaving Medicare Advantage to return to Original Medicare.

en.q: Medicare supplement policies must give buyers a free look period of at least:
o: 10 days
30 days
60 days
90 days
en.e: The buyer can return the policy for a full refund during this period. Medigap policies are also guaranteed renewable.

en.q: A 67-year-old still works for an employer with 100 employees and is covered by both the employer's group health plan and Medicare. Which generally pays first?
o: The employer's group health plan
Medicare
Whichever plan has the lower deductible
Medicaid
en.e: For employers with 20 or more employees, the group plan is primary for active workers age 65 and older, and Medicare pays second.

en.q: Long-term care that provides help with activities of daily living, often by non-medical personnel, is called:
o: Skilled care
Intermediate care
Custodial care
Acute care
en.e: Skilled care requires licensed medical professionals around the clock. Custodial care, such as help with bathing and eating, is the type most often needed.

en.q: An inflation protection option in a long-term care policy:
o: Lowers the premium by a small amount each year that the policy is held
Pays benefits only during periods of high inflation
Increases benefit amounts over time to keep pace with care costs
Ends coverage once the cost of care rises above a set dollar level
en.e: Insurers generally must offer inflation protection, and a buyer who declines it is usually asked to reject it in writing.

en.q: Under the NAIC model rules followed by most states, a long-term care policy may not:
o: Require a prior hospital stay for nursing home benefits
Include an elimination period before benefits begin
Cover care received at home from home health aides
Be issued on a guaranteed renewable basis
en.e: Policies also cannot provide significantly more coverage for skilled care than for lower levels of care, such as custodial care.

en.q: Charging different premium rates to applicants of the same class and the same life expectancy is an unfair trade practice called:
o: Rebating
Twisting
Coercion of the applicant
Unfair discrimination
en.e: Insurers may charge different rates only for legitimate differences in risk, such as age or health class.

en.q: A lender requires a borrower to buy credit life insurance from one specific insurer as a condition of approving the loan. This unfair trade practice is:
o: Coercion
Defamation
Rebating
Commingling
en.e: A borrower may be required to have insurance but generally cannot be forced to buy it from a particular insurer or producer.

en.q: Under the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, financial institutions, including insurers, must:
o: Share customer data with any outside company that requests it
Get state approval before every single insurance sale
Stop selling insurance together with banking products
Give privacy notices and let customers opt out of some data sharing
en.e: The opt-out covers sharing nonpublic personal information with nonaffiliated third parties, with some exceptions. The same law allowed banks, securities firms, and insurers to affiliate.
